d.title: Three events reach the caller and four are stored
d.caption: **The extra one is the user's own message, which ADK appends before the agent runs** — and the asymmetry is the first thing to internalise about this framework: **the stream is what you show a user, and the session is what the next turn is built from.** They are not the same list. The second column is the other half of the lesson: **nothing in the stream is “the answer” until an event says so**, which is why the loop iterates rather than awaiting a string.

d.title: Four decisions, and what each one buys
d.caption: Each of these is readable straight off the type signatures, and each one is the reason a later chapter is short. **The third is the one that surprises people: a tool does not write to a database, it writes to state, and the change rides along with the event that produced it** — so replaying the events rebuilds the state, which is what makes a session portable and an invocation resumable.

items.label: Everything is an event stream
items.desc: run_async returns an async generator, so streaming, approval and interception are events you have not consumed yet

items.label: Services are injected, not imported
items.desc: sessions, artifacts, memory and credentials are constructor arguments, so dev and production differ by one line

items.label: State changes travel with events
items.desc: a tool writes to state, the delta attaches to its event, and the service applies it on append - so replay rebuilds it

items.label: Agents compose
items.desc: an agent can hold sub-agents, be a tool, be a workflow step or be a loop body; there is no separate chain concept

d.title: Five things people expect it to be, and what it actually is
d.caption: **The last row is the one worth sitting with.** A framework cannot make an agent choose the right tool; it can only give you the hooks — callbacks, evaluation, tracing — with which to find out that it chose the wrong one. **Everything on the right is infrastructure around a model call, not an improvement to it.**

d.title: One package, two extras, and two backends chosen by environment
d.caption: **The base install is deliberately lean, and the optional pieces fail loudly rather than obscurely** — an import error that names the extra to install. The last two rows are the configuration most people get wrong on the first attempt: **the same agent code runs against both backends, and only the environment changes.** A missing variable there does not fail at import; it fails at the first model call.

d.title: What the CLI requires, and what the API requires
d.caption: **The left column is a set of conventions, not an interface** — which is the practical point of this section: a package named anything, exporting any symbol, works perfectly well in your own service. The CLI's requirements exist so that it can discover an agent without being told where it is. **And the silent one is the one that costs an afternoon: a directory with no `__init__.py` is not a package, so it is skipped without an error.**

d.title: The three objects nest, and the side effects hang off the bottom
d.caption: **Read it downwards and the whole persistence model is in one picture:** a session is keyed by three fields and holds an ordered list of events; an event records who produced it and what it carried; and an event's actions are the side effects the session service applies when the event is appended. **The actions are the part that is easy to miss and the part that does the work** — state changes, artifact versions, a transfer, an escalation, an approval request.

d.title: One runner serves every conversation, because sessions are fetched by key
d.caption: **A runner is built once at start-up and holds no conversation** — `run_async` takes the user id and the session id per call, and the session is whatever the session service returns for that key. Which is exactly what lets turn five land on a different instance from turn four. **The condition is the one in the last box: a shared session service.** With the in-memory one, two replicas means half the turns arrive at an instance that has never heard of the session.

d.title: The second tool consumes the first one's output, so the model has to chain them
d.caption: **That is the whole design of this example.** `suggest_clothing` takes a temperature and a rain chance, which only `get_forecast` can supply, so answering the question requires two tool calls in sequence and therefore three model round trips. **Nothing in the agent says so** — there is no chain, no graph and no ordering hint, only two declarations and an instruction, and the sequence is the model's inference from the parameter names.

d.title: The history grows by two blocks per tool call, and the declarations are resent every time
d.caption: **One question became three requests carrying 1, 3 and 5 content blocks** — the model's own function call and the response are both appended, and nothing is summarised or dropped. By call three it is re-reading everything it has already seen, **which is why token cost over a long tool chain grows faster than the number of calls.** The last column is the cost people forget to count: **every declaration is sent on every call, so fifty tools means fifty declarations three times over.**

d.title: Four ways an event can be the answer, and one way it looks like one
d.caption: **The rule is that an event is final when it is not partial and has no pending function calls** — plus two deliberate cases where a tool's own output is the answer, with no model pass after it. The last row is the trap worth reading twice: **in a multi-agent run one event per agent can report true**, so a front end that renders every final event shows the coordinator's answer and each specialist's. Filter by author, or take the last event of the invocation.
